source.title: A Dynamical Central Limit Theorem for Shallow Neural Networks
source.authors: Zhengdao Chen; Grant M. Rotskoff; Joan Bruna; E. Vanden-Eijnden

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling that affects the relevant findings.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes gradient-flow training of finite-width shallow networks and reports training-loss and fluctuation outcomes. Its theorem and experiments concern mean-field approximation and squared loss, rather than benchmark classification error, so they bear conceptually on the broad training claim but do not directly test the listed benchmark versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's benchmark claims about CIFAR classification, corrupted labels, spurious minima, depth and shortcuts, initialization comparisons, large learning rates, and batch normalization are cited or outside its experiments. Its own rows below cover gradient-flow training outcomes and fluctuations in shallow student networks. Figure-only trajectories and norm plots are not extracted as separate results.
record.test_reason: The study measures squared regression loss and deviations from mean-field dynamics in shallow networks. It does not test CIFAR classification, spurious-minimum frequencies as teacher and student widths grow together, depth, signal-preserving initialization, stability thresholds, or batch normalization. Its related optimization results fit none of V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate, but the vanishing-fluctuation statement needs precision: under interpolation, sufficient convergence-rate, and regularity assumptions, the long-time average of the mean-square CLT-scaled deviation vanishes after taking the width limit first. More generally, conditional long-time bounds compare deviations with Monte-Carlo resampling error and motivate regularization. These are asymptotic fluctuation guarantees, not unconditional finite-width global-convergence guarantees; extension to deep architectures remains future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses continuous-time gradient flow theory and gradient descent experiments on shallow ReLU student networks with squared population or empirical loss. It does not use the benchmark classification recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss setting and initialization vary; empirical unregularized runs drive reported training loss below 10−8, while regularized empirical runs do not vanish. Population versus empirical loss also changes the stated outcome.

fits_no_version.finding: For unregularized shallow ReLU students with either Gaussian or zero output-coefficient initialization, average empirical squared training loss and prediction fluctuation fall below 10^-8 within 1,000 iterations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Full-batch gradient descent can achieve near-zero empirical squared loss in this synthetic shallow teacher-student regression setting.

fits_no_version.finding: With regularization λ = 0.01, empirical training loss and fluctuation remain nonzero; fluctuation stays below the approximate asymptotic Monte-Carlo reference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization can leave nonzero regression loss while controlling finite-width prediction fluctuations in the tested shallow networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Population-loss trajectories are similar across student widths, and non-planted targets show qualitatively similar fluctuation behavior.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mean-field dynamics describe similar population-loss trajectories across the tested widths, with related fluctuation patterns across planted and non-planted regression targets.

record.problems: The experiments are limited to shallow networks, squared loss, and a specific synthetic student-teacher or non-planted regression setup; no classification benchmarks are tested. Reported experiments use 20 initializations, and several plotted quantities lack numerical values in the text. The central claims are asymptotic and conditional on technical assumptions.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible figure-only rows were added for fluctuation curves, neuron trajectories, TV norms, or 2-norms; these are shown in Figures 1–3 without prose values and do not measure the classification behavior in the versions.

untested.parts: All parts: convolutional classification on CIFAR-10/100, corrupted labels, SGD/Adam, and model-size, stopping, or regularization effects on classification training error.
Spurious-minimum frequency as teacher and student grow together, and the effect of adding one or two student neurons at widths 6–20. Here the teacher has two neurons and students have 128–2048.
Depth degradation, residual shortcuts, very deep plain tanh networks, and normalization-free residual training.

Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient preservation, Gaussian versus orthogonal weights, and trainable depth. Output-coefficient initialization comparisons do not test these mechanisms.
Learning rates relative to initial stability thresholds, catapult loss increases, sharpness evolution, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence.
Batch normalization comparisons, training speed, learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites original V1 and V2 sources as context. Its interpolation theorem assumes mean-field convergence to an interpolating solution. Its smoothness assumptions exclude exact ReLU units, although its numerical experiments use ReLU. Neither fact supplies a test or verdict on V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification error; random or corrupted labels; SGD or Adam; benchmark model size and training duration.
Teacher-student spurious-minimum frequency and the effect of student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual depth comparisons, shortcuts, and training at extreme depth.
Activation-matched, Gaussian, and orthogonal initialization comparisons and trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, loss spikes, sharpness, and divergence.
Batch normalization versus no normalization and corresponding speed or learning-rate tolerance.
